findings.text: Applicants often do not know how to complete the online application, including uploading documents and submitting it, which makes the first submission difficult.
Preparing the Environment Management Plan (EMP) requires specialised knowledge (material balance, effluent/waste generation, air monitoring) that an industry cannot handle on its own.
Industries depend on consultants and third-party agencies to carry out environmental studies and prepare the EMP, adding to cost and effort.
The process is not fully online, because after online submission the applicant must attend a personal meeting with the Pollution Control Board (PCB), preceded by a site visit.
Applicants must be technically prepared to answer non-conformities and observations raised at the site visit, at the committee meeting.
Any change in product mix, additional production or additional pollution generation requires a fresh CTE amendment and a subsequent CTO.
The Consent for Establishment is granted for a period of seven years; if the industry is not established within this period, a fresh consent has to be obtained.
The consent fee is linked to project cost and charged separately for air and water, with the higher of a percentage of project cost or a fixed standard amount being payable for each.
No exact time limit is defined by the PCB for issuing the consent, as the time depends on the number of applications received.
Guidelines and requirements are amended from time to time, and industries need awareness of the current requirements.
The EMP covers proposed products with material balance, raw materials and quantities, water input, effluent (high and low TDS), and solid/solvent wastes.
After the site visit, the PCB records observations/non-conformities in an agenda shared with the industry so it can prepare answers for the committee meeting.
Participants did not report any unnecessary or duplicate documents and stated all documents requested are required.
The time taken depends on the number of applications received each month, since the committee meets only twice a month and disposes of about 20 to 25 applications per meeting.
The overall process takes about three to six months; one participant reported their consent took six months.
Site inspection takes place two to three weeks after application; the certificate is then issued about two to three weeks after the meeting.
The competent authority should provide training to industry employees on using the online portal, uploading documents and submitting applications.
Provide a clear checklist of documents/information required, and clear communication on timelines for inspection, meeting and certificate issuance.
Participants described PCB officials as cooperative, with observations resolved through clarification rather than friction.
Example cited: for a project cost of ₹50 lakh, the higher of the percentage-based amount (~₹37,500) and the standard amount (₹50,000) is payable for each of air and water, totalling ₹1,00,000.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

gaps.text: ED states CTE is fully digital end-to-end with a committed 28-day turnaround and no offline/manual applications accepted (applicantOfficeVisit: no); FGD participants describe CTE as 'a hybrid process' requiring a mandatory site visit and personal meeting with the PCB committee, and report the overall process taking three to six months (one case cited at six months), with the committee meeting only twice a month to dispose of 20–25 applications.

ED's CTE record states no fixed validity period was discussed and describes CTE only as a 'one-time' pre-establishment consent; FGD participants state the Consent for Establishment is explicitly granted for a fixed seven-year validity period, after which a fresh consent must be obtained if the industry has not been established.

FGD participants did not mention the deemed-approval provision for CTE at all; ED had stated this provision exists (though never invoked), so the FGD does not corroborate or contradict its operational status.

FGD participants reported PCB officials as cooperative and did not flag any documents as unnecessary or duplicate for CTE, a notably positive operational assessment of the PCB component of the process.

findings.text: The CTO process is only partly online: after the online application, applicants must still go through a personal site inspection and personal interaction with the PCB and its committee.
Industry representatives must appear before a multi-department committee that asks many technical questions difficult to answer without expert help.

Even qualified staff (graduates, postgraduates, doctorate holders) find it hard to answer some environmental questions, as environmental science is a specialised subject, so continuing expert support is felt necessary.

Applicants do not receive real-time tracking or email/SMS alerts and must keep calling and coordinating with the authorities to learn application status; the outcome is announced only at the committee meeting.
Increasing the number of products, even without raising sanctioned production capacity or effluent load, requires an amendment to the CTE followed by a fresh CTO — described as a repeating cycle.
Applicants are unsure of the likely amount of analysis charges and penalties, which depend on PCB sampling and on bank guarantees imposed by the Board.
Participants stated that a circular or government order requires a consultant to accompany the industry representative to the committee, making consultancy effectively mandatory for CTO.
The consent fee follows a structure based on project cost, with rates differing across red, orange and green categories (red being highest).
The validity of the CTO depends on compliance history, ranging from five years for smoothly running industries to one or two years where there are complaints or frequent violations.
The CTO application requires employee details to be submitted again and everything from the CFE (plant, raw materials, process with inputs/outputs) to be restated.
At the committee meeting the application is recorded as approved, deferred (further information required, resubmit at next meeting) or rejected.

The PCB can collect samples from the factory at any time, including surprise night inspections; the applicant pays analysis charges directly, and exceeding permitted ranges can trigger a penalty or a bank guarantee.
Information already submitted for the CTE (employee details, plant, raw materials, process details) must be stated again in the CTO application.
The overall process takes three to six months, with three months as the minimum; the committee meets only twice a month, so the number of applications received affects waiting time.
Inspection dates and application status are not communicated through the portal, so progress depends on frequent personal follow-up with the authorities.
Provide real-time tracking of CTO applications with email and SMS alerts, and increase the frequency of committee meetings or process applications on a rolling basis.
Simplify the procedure for increasing the number of products within the sanctioned production capacity and effluent load, so the full CFE-and-CTO cycle is not repeated.
Make information on fees, analysis charges and penalties easily available to applicants in advance.

The consent fee for the full five-year validity can be paid in instalments (e.g. ₹1 lakh per year on a ₹5 lakh total), a facility available to all industries; no separate fee is charged for periodic PCB inspections.

gaps.text: ED states CTO takes roughly two weeks (14 days) from application with no applicant office visit required (applicantOfficeVisit: no); FGD participants describe the process taking three to six months (minimum three months) and say it is 'not completely online' because it requires a personal site inspection and personal interaction with the PCB committee, with a GO reportedly making a consultant's presence mandatory.

ED states PCB consent under CTO is 'commonly issued for around 2 years and must be renewed separately'; FGD participants describe CTO validity as generally five years for smoothly-running industries, reduced to one or two years only where there are complaints or violations.
ED flagged deemed approval for CTO as unclear/unconfirmed; FGD does not mention deemed approval for CTO at all, so the ambiguity remains unresolved.
FGD confirms the CTO fee for the five-year validity can be paid in yearly instalments (e.g. ₹1 lakh/year on a ₹5 lakh total) — a practical flexibility not mentioned in the ED record.

findings.text: Setback requirements become difficult to meet where an industrial unit is surrounded by other industries or residential houses, and deviations may be needed.
A fixed minimum set of documents is mandatory for every application, with no shortcut even where some requested data appears unnecessary to applicants.
Approval involves several separate authorities and steps — the land-allotting authority, the factory inspectorate and the pollution control board — each with its own requirements.
Dependence on contractors and consultants, including chemical consultancy, to navigate the approval process adds to cost and effort.
The actual time taken can be considerably longer than the prescribed period, with one participant citing about a year or more in some cases.
Setback norms do not provide a simple route for units surrounded by residential or other industrial development; such cases depend on deviations being granted.
Norms such as the 10% greenery requirement are fixed by the authority at the time of land allotment and must be complied with.
The pollution control board follows its own policy and rules, separate from the authority granting building approval, even though both fall under the State Government.
Participants felt reform initiatives announced by the Central and State Governments are not always reflected in practice on the ground.

The factory building plan is submitted to the land-allotting authority through a common platform, where the plan and building cost are assessed, fees paid online, and compliance with setbacks and other rules checked.

For red category industries, PCB inspection and permission is required; a unit identified as green category at the time of allotment can receive PCB permission directly, with only an inspection involved.
Inspections and prescribed documentation cannot be avoided, and building approval and pollution board clearance run as separate processes (no single consolidated certificate).
No specific duplicate document issue was raised in detail, though one participant felt some requested data is unnecessary while another maintained it is the minimum required.
Participants discussed that the factory inspector, pollution control board and building approval processes run separately and could potentially be combined to reduce repeated submissions.
The prescribed timeline for approval is short (about 20 days was mentioned), but actual completion takes longer in practice.
Delays arise from inspections and clearances that must be completed by separate departments, such as the factory inspectorate and the pollution control board.
Explore clubbing the related approvals (building plan approval, factory inspectorate and pollution control board clearance) into a more integrated process.
Extend the practice of identifying the industry category at the time of land allotment, so pollution board permission can follow directly where the unit is green category.
Ensure announced reforms are implemented effectively on the ground through a single, uniformly working online system, with the GST portal cited as a model.
One participant reported facing no difficulty applying and described the documentation as the minimum data that has to be provided.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: We did not face any difficulty in applying; the documentation asked for is the minimum data we need to provide, and it is all mandatory.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Setbacks are a concern only in rare cases, where the industry is surrounded by other industries or residential houses and a deviation from the setbacks is needed.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The pollution board is separate and follows its own rules; if the unit is identified as green category at the time of land allotment, the pollution board permission can be given directly and only the inspection is involved.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The prescribed time is around 20 days, but in practice the process can take much longer, in some cases about a year.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Central and State Governments say they are working in coordination on reforms, but on the ground it is just eyewash; reforms should actually work, like the GST portal.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: For this process, businesses end up depending on contractors and consultants, including chemical consultancy.

gaps.text: No specific document checklist was given beyond participants' general reference to a 'fixed minimum set' of mandatory documents.
No specific fee amount or formula was given beyond a general statement that fees are linked to the built-up area of the proposed building.
Actual processing time was reported as ranging up to about a year in some cases, against a prescribed ~20-day timeline, but no precise distribution or typical duration was given.
Deemed approval was not discussed by participants for Factory Building Plan Approval.

Participants suggested combining building plan approval, factory inspectorate and PCB clearance into a single integrated process, and extending category identification at land allotment so green-category units get direct PCB permission.

Units identified as green category at the time of land allotment can reportedly receive PCB permission directly with only an inspection, bypassing the fuller clearance route required for red category units.

remarks: This FGD session combined perspectives on Factory Building Plan Approval with related approvals (factory inspectorate, pollution control board); only findings specific to building plan approval are recorded here.
Record is FGD-only and has not been verified against an official ED interview; timeline, fee and document details are as described by business participants and may be incomplete or approximate.
Participants compared Telangana's ease of doing business with other states, such as Gujarat, Odisha and Bihar, without providing specific comparative detail.

findings.text: Participants found the current online process much easier than the earlier offline system.
Officer availability and inspection/stamping scheduling were identified as the main practical constraint, especially for plants located far from the city.
For repair cases requiring a government seal to be opened, approval still involves coordination with the department and, in some cases, physical follow-up.
Delay in inspection or stamping is operationally significant because the affected dispenser or equipment cannot be used until the approval/stamping is completed.
Repeated re-stamping can add to the cost of compliance, particularly for equipment with multiple nozzles or units.
Registration is a one-time/perpetual requirement, while stamping is carried out periodically, generally on a yearly basis for the instruments discussed.
Timely completion of application and payment may still result in compliance gaps where inspection or stamping is delayed by departmental scheduling, including beyond the applicable validity period.
Businesses face challenges keeping track of frequent changes/amendments under Legal Metrology and the Packaged Commodities Rules.
Repair-related cases may require letters from the company/dealer and approval/signature before the repair and re-sealing can proceed.
Participants indicated the repair/approval workflow could be shifted fully online, with machine details, serial numbers and supporting documents submitted through the system.

For repair cases, coordinating multiple letters/documents from the company, dealer and other parties before approval was identified as an area that could be simplified through digital submission and e-signatures.
The most relevant delay factor discussed was availability of the inspecting officer, especially for plants located far from the city.
Actual inspection or approval can often happen quickly once the concerned officer is available; the difficulty is primarily scheduling and dependency on availability.
Introduce deemed approval for cases where the applicant applied and paid within the required period but inspection/stamping is delayed for reasons not attributable to them.
Allow a defined 15-day grace period after expiry, without additional charges, where the compliance process was initiated in time.
Review and rationalise re-stamping charges, particularly where only one nozzle/unit of a larger dispenser is affected, and consider a rebate for re-stamping done soon after original stamping.
Publish regular updates, guidance notes and awareness material on changes to Legal Metrology requirements and the Packaged Commodities Rules.
Consultants/agents are still used in some locations mainly because of operational workload and the need to coordinate slots and departmental visits; other users complete applications themselves.
Industry raised a broader concern about maintaining a reasonable balance between enforcement and the practical realities of businesses operating on relatively small margins.

gaps.text: ED's fee figures (~₹5,000 in one context; ~₹500 for packer registration) do not capture informal/intermediary costs; FGD participants cite needing to go through agencies at a cost of roughly ₹25,000 in some cases — an additional cost not reflected in the ED record.

ED did not detail a periodic stamping/re-verification cycle; FGD participants describe stamping (distinct from one-time registration) as carried out periodically, generally yearly, for the instruments discussed.

FGD does not quantify how long inspection/repair-approval delays typically last beyond noting that affected equipment is kept out of service; no day-level figures are given, consistent with the ED's own lack of day-level timeline detail for Legal Metrology.

findings.text: Industries depend heavily on consultants, with participants estimating that 60 to 70 per cent of industries use them from the application stage until the certificate is issued.
Industries do not receive alerts, SMS or emails about new circulars, public notices and notifications, which are published only on the website.
Where a company has expanded, renewal requires a fresh Chartered Accountant certificate of project cost, and a fee must be paid on the increase in project cost.
A change of product or an expansion during the validity period requires a fresh CTE followed by a CTO, run separately from the renewal and tracked/renewed separately.
Any discharge or emission complaint found during PCB monitoring can lead to the case being referred to a task force committee, a bank guarantee and, in serious cases, a stop-production order.
The renewal process is not fully online, as industries must still go through an inspection and attend a personal meeting.
The CTO is granted for five years, and the renewal application must be submitted online at least six months before the existing CTO expires, with the prescribed fee.
The renewal fee is the same as the CTO fee, and an additional fee is charged on any increase in project cost since the last grant (e.g. a rise of ₹15–20 crore cited).

Environmental Clearance (EC) is a separate, mandatory approval for CTE unless the industrial estate has already obtained EC for the entire estate; industries on private land outside an estate must obtain their own EC, reviewed by the state office and sanctioned by the ministry in Delhi.

The renewal application must include the compliance report on Schedule B and C conditions, the EMP, and production details of the last six months, plus effluent, water input and hazardous waste/equipment details.
The renewal must include a copy of the agreement with the common treatment facility where high-TDS effluent is sent for treatment.

If there is any change in product, the applicant must start again from the Consent for Establishment, and any expansion during renewal is treated as a new, separate consent not included in the renewal.

Complaints on discharge/emissions found during PCB monitoring are referred to a task force committee, which can require a bank guarantee (e.g. ₹5–10 lakh) before operations continue, and a stop-production order if the violation occurs during the licence period.
Some departments hold virtual meetings, but participants felt personal attendance is needed for this service to explain matters properly.
Participants did not identify any unnecessary documents for renewal, naming the compliance report, EMP, production details and consumption details as the required set.
Participants did not report any delay or rejection in their own renewals, stating the process runs as usual.
A change of product or expansion requires a fresh Consent for Establishment, adding a separate approval cycle in addition to the renewal.
Applicants who are not aware of recent circulars or amended requirements may have to correct or resubmit their applications.
Authorities should provide proper training to industry staff, so applications can be prepared and submitted without relying on consultants.
Provide timely alerts through SMS or email on circulars, notifications and public notices, and strengthen communication through industry associations.
Allow minor changes in product mix within the permitted quantity to be handled more directly, without repeating the full Consent for Establishment cycle.

Participants suggested industry associations also be consulted, as they are aware of latest problems and submit representations to departments, though participants noted gaps in communication from associations to their members.

Specific fee amounts (renewal fee, additional fee on project-cost increase, exact bank-guarantee amounts beyond the cited ₹5–10 lakh range) were not given precisely.

findings.text: The requirement to install fire safety infrastructure (fire exits, openings, firewalls, separate dedicated water tanks and pipelines) is costly, even for lower-height industrial and commercial buildings.
Industries must manage several separate applications and portals for different services, with no single dashboard to track all services in one place.
Payment gateway charges are levied on online fee payments, adding to the cost of the service.
Details already submitted to the government (Aadhaar, company details, building approvals) have to be entered or uploaded again for each application.
Deficiencies in documents are raised as a shortfall, and the site inspection and compliance with its observations can extend the renewal beyond the expected time.
Industries are not always aware of the fire safety requirements, and basic training on fire safety is needed.
The Fire NOC requirement depends on building height/type, applying from about 10 metres for commercial/industrial buildings versus about 15 metres for residential buildings.
Validity depends on the structure; for some buildings it is one year, so the NOC has to be renewed regularly.
Penalties are calculated based on the height, width and area of the building.
Participants felt that for industrial/commercial buildings of about 10 to 15 metres, fire cylinders (extinguishers) should be accepted in place of heavy fire structures.

The renewal application is submitted online on the fire department's website (available at all times) with required documents (building plan approval, occupancy certificate, Aadhaar, company details, fire design).
If any document is missing, the department raises a shortfall that the applicant must resolve before the process continues.
A site inspection is carried out within about 10 to 15 days, checking fire exits, openings, firewalls, tanks and firefighting equipment; the certificate is issued once the department is satisfied.

Participants described a sequence of pre-construction (building plan, fire design) and post-construction (occupancy, consent for operation) approvals, and wanted these handled through a single window.
Aadhaar, company registration details and building plan approvals already submitted to government should be fetched automatically instead of being uploaded again.
Applications to different departments (fire, groundwater, electricity, building plan approval) require similar information to be submitted separately to each.
Renewal is expected to take about one week; delay is felt beyond seven days, with cases of about 12 days mentioned.
Site inspection typically takes place 10 to 15 days after application, and shortfalls found during inspection must be rectified before the certificate is issued.
Provide a single dashboard where all services can be applied for, tracked and paid for in one place, and introduce a mobile application with SMS notifications.
Remove or reduce payment gateway charges on online payments of fees.
Allow self-certification through a single application shared with all departments concerned.
Larger companies generally use consultants, while the renewal itself is a relatively simple process.

findings.text: The process takes a long time, with participants citing a minimum of about 45 days for a new water connection, considered a main concern.
Industry staff who handle the application are often unaware of the procedure and untrained, so they usually depend on outside agents or consultants.
Connection charges, including civil works and road cutting/restoration, can be substantial and depend on the size of the connection and pipeline distance.
Applicants cannot easily estimate the total cost in advance, as the amounts depend on pipe size, civil work required and the contractor.
In rural areas and during summer, water supply is insufficient (borewells run dry, municipal water released only on alternate days) even where a pipeline exists.
The granting authority depends on jurisdiction — the Hyderabad Metro Water Supply and Sewerage Board in its area or the rural water supply department elsewhere.
Connection is granted based on water requirement stated in kilolitres per day (KLD); pipeline vs groundwater option depends on a feasibility report.
Participants felt the timeline for approval and physical connection should be clearly defined, since time is important for industries starting operations.
Connectivity for rural industries is a concern because the availability of piped water is limited.
The application is submitted online with building permission, occupancy certificate and an authorisation letter from the concerned authorised person of the company.
The applicant states the water requirement in KLD; the authority then inspects the site and prepares a feasibility report on pipeline connection versus groundwater.
After inspection, approval is given in about seven days; connection charges are then paid according to connection size.
Connection work is carried out through a contractor, taking about one to three days after approval depending on pipeline distance; afterwards, water charges are billed and paid monthly.
One participant raised the amount of documentation required online as a challenge, but no specific duplicate or unnecessary document was identified.
The minimum time of about 45 days is taken up by inspection, feasibility report and approval, ranging from about a week to a month for individual steps depending on the authority's schedule.
Delay can arise where the pipeline is far from the site, since connection work depends on the distance of the pipeline and on the contractor.
Companies unaware of the procedure, or that apply late, lose time, since the connection should be sought at the initial stage before starting operations.
Set and publish clear timelines for the approval of the application, the inspection and the physical connection.
Provide training and guidance to company staff on the water connection procedure, so they can apply without depending on outside agents.
Make connection charges (civil, pipeline, road restoration) transparent and available in advance.
Improve water supply and connectivity for rural industries and during summer.
Application fees were described as nil or minimal at the start, with the main costs arising later as connection charges.

No fixed overall approval timeline was confirmed by the authority; participants cited a minimum of about 45 days, with individual steps ranging from about a week to a month depending on schedule.
